Bimetallic Single Atom Catalysts for Biomass Valorization to Sustainable Fuels

Bryant Montenegro · MSc Sustainable Energy · Hamad Bin Khalifa University

01BACKGROUND / WHY IT MATTERS

01The problem

Aviation is hard to electrify

Batteries are still too heavy for most flights, especially long ones, so aircraft will keep needing energy-dense liquid fuels. Those fuels have to come from somewhere other than fossil oil.

02The opportunity

The carbon is already in waste

Farm and forestry waste contains hemicellulose, and furfural is already made from it industrially. A renewable building block exists today, not just on paper.

03The gap

Too small to fly

Furfural is a small C₅ molecule. Jet fuel is made of longer chains of roughly C₈–C₁₆, so two furfurals have to be joined first.

04This project

Join them with electricity

Electroreduction on a bimetallic single-atom catalyst couples two furfurals into C₁₀ hydrofuroin, a step toward jet-range fuel.

This page deliberately leaves out market, demand and emissions figures. For those, see the IEA and IATA.

step 1 / 7

    Schematic, not a simulation; adsorption geometry and timing are illustrative. If a ketyl radical takes a second e⁻ and H⁺ instead of coupling, the product is furfuryl alcohol, the main competing pathway.

    step 1 / 6

      Schematic cross-sections, not to scale. Both cells share one timeline to compare how the chemistry flows; molecule counts are illustrative and say nothing about relative performance.

      Flow cell

      • Furfural is delivered to the catalyst by forced flow, not by diffusion and stirring alone.
      • Better control of mass transport at the electrode surface.
      • Larger electrode area and room to run at higher current.
      • Zero-gap stack: ions cross only the membrane, with no liquid gap between the electrodes.
      • Continuous recirculation; product collects in an external reservoir for sampling.
      • Closer to the design needed for scale-up and sustained production.

      H-cell is still the tool for

      • Fast catalyst screening with simple hardware.
      • Precise potential control against a reference electrode.

      Still to be evaluated

      Cell voltage, energy use, membrane transport and catalyst stability in the flow cell.

      The H-cell finds the catalyst and conditions; the flow cell tests whether better transport, larger area and recirculation can raise hydrofuroin production.

      step 1 / 6

        Schematic, not a simulation. Shows one plausible full-HDO sequence (ring saturation, then C–OH hydrogenolysis, then ring opening); the real order, intermediates and product mix (for example cyclic or partly deoxygenated C₁₀) depend on the catalyst and conditions. The catalyst is a generic bifunctional metal–acid type commonly used for HDO in the literature (metal for hydrogenation, acid sites for C–O cleavage); FeNi–N–C is not used for this step.

        A Scientific Visualization

        About the model

        What it shows

        A schematic of FeNi–N–C: nitrogen-doped graphene holding isolated Fe–N₄ and Ni–N₄ sites, shown as one patch of a hollow carbon nanosphere, plus two reaction schemes, furfural → hydrofuroin → n-decane.

        Lattice

        • One flat graphene layer with C–C = 1.42 Å and no relaxation, so M–N comes out at 1.88 Å (relaxed ≈ 1.9–2.0 Å) and pyrrolic C–N at about 1.5 Å (real ≈ 1.38 Å).
        • Metals: M1 and M2 can each be Fe, Ni, Cu or Co (picker in the top bar), because the metal pair is still under investigation; Fe–Ni is only the default. All metals use the same drawn geometry (M–N 1.88 Å); only colour, label and HAADF brightness (Z) change.
        • Fe and Ni each sit in a divacancy, bonded to four pyridinic N in the plane. The Tilt view shows that the site is planar.
        • Graphitic N replaces one C; pyridinic N lines a single vacancy; pyrrolic N closes a five-membered ring on a hole edge and carries an H.
        • Sites are placed at random from a fixed seed. Counts come from the Adjust panel, not from measurements.
        • Charge density is a qualitative sketch from electronegativity: N is shaded δ− (electron-rich); C next to N and the metal centres are shaded δ+ (electron-poor). The shading is qualitative only. It is not from DFT or Bader analysis.

        HAADF simulation

        • Each atom adds a Gaussian probe spot weighted by Z1.7, the usual approximate Z-contrast scaling; one layer only, with shot-noise-like noise and a gamma curve.
        • Probe sizes are presets, not fitted to a particular instrument's transfer function.

        Nanosphere

        • Illustrative: shell layers, dopant density and the highlighted patch are not to scale.

        Reaction tabs

        • Electroreduction: one e⁻ and one H⁺ per furfural give ketyl radicals that couple into hydrofuroin. Adsorption on Fe and on Ni is illustrative.
        • Competing view: furfuryl alcohol (second e⁻ and H⁺) and H₂ evolution (Volmer, then Heyrovsky) drawn beside coupling; no selectivities are implied.
        • Compare sites view: isolated Fe–N₄, isolated Ni–N₄ and an Fe–Ni pair, illustrating the dual-site hypothesis.
        • Reactor: a three-compartment H-cell (RHE, working and counter compartments, membrane between WE and CE) beside a zero-gap MEA flow cell, on one shared timeline. It shows how the chemistry flows in each setup: reactant delivery, half-reactions, ion and electron paths, product handling. The anode reaction (O₂ evolution) is assumed; no performance values are shown.
        • Hydrodeoxygenation: one plausible full-HDO sequence over a generic bifunctional metal–acid catalyst (Pt metal sites for H₂ activation and hydrogenation, acid sites for dehydration and C–O cleavage), with H₂ as the H source. FeNi–N–C is not used for this step; the HDO catalyst in the thesis is still under investigation. The real order, intermediates and products depend on the catalyst and conditions.
        • Geometry and timing are drawn, not computed, and no energies are shown.

        References

        1. A. H. Castro Neto et al., “The electronic properties of graphene”, Rev. Mod. Phys. 81, 109 (2009). Graphene lattice and C–C bond length.
        2. S. J. Pennycook, D. E. Jesson, “High-resolution Z-contrast imaging of crystals”, Ultramicroscopy 37, 14 (1991). Z-contrast in HAADF-STEM.
        3. O. L. Krivanek et al., “Atom-by-atom structural and chemical analysis by annular dark-field electron microscopy”, Nature 464, 571 (2010). Single-atom ADF contrast in doped graphene.
        4. G. W. Huber, J. N. Chheda, C. J. Barrett, J. A. Dumesic, “Production of liquid alkanes by aqueous-phase processing of biomass-derived carbohydrates”, Science 308, 1446 (2005). Bifunctional metal–acid (Pt on acidic support) HDO of biomass-derived C–C coupled intermediates to alkanes.
        5. A. Zitolo et al., “Identification of catalytic sites for oxygen reduction in iron- and nitrogen-doped graphene materials”, Nat. Mater. 14, 937 (2015). Fe–N₄ sites in N-doped graphene.
